title: No-Knead Bread - Classic Version
description:
This is one of the most amazing recipes that we have come upon and actively use. It is the most wonderful bread that we have ever made at home. And, it’s very easy – assuming you do just a little bit of planning!
This recipe first appeared in an article in The New York Times, by the “Minimalist,” Mark Bittman, in November 2006. As he said, “Innovations in bread baking are rare. In fact, the 6,000-year-old process hasn’t changed much since Pasteur made the commercial production of standardized yeast possible in 1859.” (Sliced bread doesn’t count as a great innovation!)
The revolutionary nature of this bread is, of course, no kneading (though we’ve always enjoyed that part of bread making). The idea is to let the yeast do all the work by letting the dough rise overnight.
The bread comes out with a wonderful crust and a nice chewy interior.
So take a few minutes the day before you want to make this and you’ll enjoy the best bread you’ll ever make at home. It’s better than many loaves you can buy in stores (except in little, hard-to-find villages in France).
START TO FINISH: 16-24 HOURS
ingredients: ¼ oz instant or rapid-rise yeast
directions: In a large bowl, combine flour, yeast and salt. Add 1 5/8 cups water, and stir until blended; dough will be shaggy and sticky.
Cover bowl with plastic wrap or lid. Let dough rest at least 12 hours, preferably about 18, at warm room temperature.
Cover with lid and bake 30 minutes, then remove lid and bake another 15 to 30 minutes, until loaf is beautifully browned. Cool on a rack.
Cover with a cotton napkin or towel and let rise for about 2 hours. When it is ready, dough will be more than double in size and will not readily spring back when poked with a finger.
At least a half-hour before dough is ready, heat oven to 450 degrees. Put a 6- to 8-quart heavy covered pot (cast iron, enamel, Pyrex or ceramic) in oven as it heats.

When dough is ready, carefully remove pot from oven. Pick up the sides of the parchment paper with the dough and put it all into pot. Shake pan once or twice if dough is unevenly distributed; it will straighten out as it bakes.

Dough is ready when its surface is dotted with bubbles. Lightly flour a work surface and place dough on it; sprinkle it with a little more flour and fold it over on itself once or twice. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let rest about 15 minutes.

Using just enough flour to keep dough from sticking to work surface or to your fingers, gently and quickly shape dough into a ball. Sprinkle a generous sheet of parchment paper with a little flour or cornmeal; put dough seam side down on paper.
